zh.title: 推理时计算：从多采样到验证与预算分配
zh.summary: 让模型对同一道题多花一些计算，怎样才更容易答对？主读比较几种做法：从头独立做多遍、看着之前的解答继续修改，以及边做边检查步骤。选读 Self-Consistency、Let’s Verify Step by Step 和 STaR，分别解释怎样投票选答案、怎样训练负责检查的模型，以及怎样把生成的解答变成训练数据。先分清“这一次多尝试几次”和“训练以后更会做题”，再读实验和成本比较。可以先从 Self-Consistency 的算术例子开始。

en.title: Test-time compute: sampling, verification, and budget allocation
en.summary: The main ICLR 2025 reading explains sequential revision, parallel sampling, verifier search, and how difficulty and compute accounting shape the conclusions. Optional readings on Self-Consistency, Let’s Verify Step by Step, and STaR develop voting, process supervision, and training-time bootstrapping. Concrete examples distinguish spending more compute on one request from learning to solve future requests better. Start with Self-Consistency if these concepts are new.

papers.title: Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally Can be More Effective than Scaling Parameters for Reasoning

zh.contribution: 同一道题，模型可以多试几种解法，也可以反复修改上一份答案，还可以边写边检查。论文比较了这些做法，发现怎样花计算量更划算，取决于题目对模型有多难，以及允许它尝试多少次。
zh.relevance: 帮助理解“让模型多想一会儿”具体怎样实现，以及为什么有时有效、有时越改越错。对推理服务而言，这些做法还会带来不同的等待时间、显存占用和检查答案的额外开销。
zh.reading: 本期主读，值得精读。先跟着同一道几何题，理解重新作答、连续修改和检查中间步骤的区别；再看实验如何比较它们。最后的公式可以先跳过，不影响理解主要结论。建议 40–60 分钟。
zh.prerequisites: 正文从一次模型调用讲起：模型收到题目，逐段生成解答，再输出最终答案。文中会依次解释评分模型、单次答对率和计算量的计数方法，不需要先学过强化学习算法。
zh.caveat: 论文先让模型大量试答来估计题目难度，却没有把这部分计算计入主要收益。文中的 4× 也不是 GPU 实测快四倍；能否胜过参数多 14 倍的模型，还取决于题目难度和上线后要回答多少问题。

sections.heading: 同一道题，让模型多做几次，怎样做才有用
paragraphs: 模型收到一道题，生成解答，这个过程叫推理。假设第一次没有答对，而我们愿意再花一些计算量：可以只把原题再发一次，让它重新做；也可以连同上次的解答一起发过去，让它修改；还可以写几步就检查一次，决定从哪里继续。Snell、Lee、Xu、Kumar 的论文比较的就是这些选择，以及它们各自在什么情况下更有效。[ICLR 2025 正式记录](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/hash/1b623663fd9b874366f3ce019fdfdd44-Abstract-Conference.html)
下面用同一道“求三角形面积”的几何题贯穿解释，假设可以作辅助线，也可以建立坐标来解。**这是帮助理解执行过程的例子，不是论文中的实验题。** 多尝试几次，也许能得到一份正确解答；但系统还得认出它，才能交给用户。论文始终在处理这两个问题：怎样产生更好的解答，以及怎样从几份解答里选对。

这项工作先以预印本形式发表于 2024 年，随后成为 ICLR 2025 会议论文。预印本标题以 Scaling Model Parameters 结尾，会议版改为 Scaling Parameters for Reasoning。下文的图号和计算量说明以会议版为准，因为它补充了检查答案所需的计算开销。[预印本](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.03314)；[正式版 §2](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/file/1b623663fd9b874366f3ce019fdfdd44-Paper-Conference.pdf#page=3)

sections.heading: 先把两件事分开：怎样写下一份解答，怎样检查解答
paragraphs: 先看模型怎样作答。只给它同一道几何题，并使用带随机性的生成方式，它可能这次作辅助线，下次建立坐标，也可能仍然写出相似解法。若把“上一份坐标解法”也放进输入，模型下一次看到的信息就变了，它有机会沿着原解法纠错。论文把各种解答被生成出来的可能性称为 proposal distribution；所谓改变这个分布，在这里就是通过改变输入，让下一次作答更可能朝有用的方向走。[正式版 §2–3](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/file/1b623663fd9b874366f3ce019fdfdd44-Paper-Conference.pdf#page=3)
再看系统怎样选择。一个直接做法是让模型独立写 N 份完整解答，再用另一个模型给它们打分，挑一份提交；这叫 best-of-N，N 就是尝试次数。负责打分的模型叫 verifier，即验证器。也可以不用等整份解答写完，而是检查已经写出的步骤，只让得分较好的解法继续。这样既要考虑解题模型会写什么，也要考虑检查模型会保留什么。
本文的修正能力是提前训练出来的。回答一道新题时，模型会把旧答案放进输入，但不会为这道题重新训练、修改权重。作者确实把“修改答案”和“给完整答案打分”结合使用了；更复杂的“反复修改，同时对每一步展开搜索”，则不能当作本文已经一起验证过的方法。

sections.heading: 还是这道几何题：16 次作答可以怎样安排
paragraphs: **继续使用教学例子，假设最多允许写出 16 份完整解答。** 第一种安排是只给原题，独立作答 16 次，最后选一份。各次尝试不读取彼此的答案，所以可以并行执行。这给了模型多次重新选择解题路线的机会，通常称为并行采样。
第二种安排是先答一次，再连续修改 15 次，共得到 16 份解答。后一次必须读前一次的结果，因此要按顺序执行，称为串行修正。第三种安排折中：先独立开始四次，每次都继续修改三次，得到四条各含四份解答的链，也就是 4×4。这里的一次始终指一份完整解答，不是一行推理步骤。

如果一开始选错了几何思路，连续修改可能始终绕不出去，多次从头做更有机会换到合适的路线。如果思路已经正确，只是最后算面积时出错，修改旧答案可能更有效。这是帮助理解实验的直觉，模型实际修正时也可能完全换一种解法。无论采用哪种安排，都仍需挑选答案；而且这 16 次作答的长度、输入历史和检查费用可能不同，暂时不能说它们耗时一样。[正式版 Fig. 5、7](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/file/1b623663fd9b874366f3ce019fdfdd44-Paper-Conference.pdf#page=7)

sections.heading: 怎样给没写完的解答打分
paragraphs: 要在几何解答写到一半时决定是否继续，需要一个能给中间步骤打分的模型。这类模型叫过程奖励模型，英文缩写 PRM。本文训练它的方法是：保留一道题已经写出的前几步，让解题模型从这里继续做多次，统计最后有多少次答对，再让 PRM 学会预测这个比例。反复采样来估计结果的方法称为 Monte Carlo。附录 F 的具体设置是每道训练题取 16 份解答，在每个步骤处再做 16 次续写。[正式版 §5.1、附录 F](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/file/1b623663fd9b874366f3ce019fdfdd44-Paper-Conference.pdf#page=19)
所以，这里的分数回答的是：“按照当前解题模型的能力，从这几步往下做，最终做对的可能性有多大？”它没有直接证明这些步骤在数学上正确。分数来自有限次尝试，PRM 自身的预测也会出错；若把高分当成正确性的保证，后面的搜索就可能被它带偏。

等一份解答写完，作者用 PRM 在最后一步给出的分数代表整份解答，再把得到相同最终答案的分数相加。**仍以求面积为例，仅示意选择规则：**两份解答都得到 12，各得 0.6 分；另一份得到 10，得 0.9 分。前者合计 1.2，系统会选择 12。这叫 best-of-N weighted，即按评分加权选择；直接挑单份最高分会选 10，而普通多数投票则只数票数、不看分数。[附录 G](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/file/1b623663fd9b874366f3ce019fdfdd44-Paper-Conference.pdf#page=20)

sections.heading: 边写边检查，为什么也会越做越差
paragraphs: 有了中间步骤的分数，就能这样解题：先让模型写出几种开头，给它们评分，只保留较好的几种；再从保留下来的解答各写出一些后续步骤，继续评分和筛选。这个过程叫 beam search，通常译为束搜索。与每份解答都写到最后才检查相比，它希望更早停止不值得继续的尝试。[正式版 Fig. 2、§5.2–5.3、附录 C](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/file/1b623663fd9b874366f3ce019fdfdd44-Paper-Conference.pdf#page=5)
还有一种做法叫 lookahead：暂时往后写 k 步，看看写下去是否仍然有希望，再决定保不保留当前这条解法。但试写的部分也消耗计算。论文在比较时把它近似记成 N(k+1)，其中 N 是原有生成预算，k 是额外试写的步数。这里要理解的重点是：多看几步可能帮助判断，但不能把这些试写当作免费。
Fig. 3 显示，在较小预算下，beam search 有优势；预算增大后，优势会缩小，有些设置甚至不如独立写完再选。作者观察到重复却没增加信息的步骤，以及过短的解答，认为模型可能更擅长取得评分器喜欢的分数，却没有更接近正确答案。这是该实验对评分错误的警示，不代表所有逐步搜索方法都会失败。

sections.heading: 模型为什么会修改答案，又为什么会把对的改错
paragraphs: 要让模型利用旧解答，作者先专门教它做修正。每道训练题生成 64 个回答，从中取最多四个错误回答作为输入，再把一个正确回答作为希望模型写出的目标。作者还会挑文字上较相关的错误解答，让“看完旧答案再修改”这件事更有意义；使用的编辑距离，就是衡量两段文字要改动多少才能变成彼此。实际回答新题时只保留最近四次作答，因此即使连续修改很多次，也不必把全部历史都放进输入。[正式版 §6.1、附录 L](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/file/1b623663fd9b874366f3ce019fdfdd44-Paper-Conference.pdf#page=24)

问题在于，训练时模型看到的是“前面有错，接下来改对”；真正使用时，前一次可能已经正确。两种情况不一样，模型却可能仍继续改。论文报告，在这个设置中约 38% 的正确答案被改成了错误答案。所以不能把第 16 次作答直接当成最终结果，必须回看中间已经得到的答案。[正式版 §6.1](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/file/1b623663fd9b874366f3ce019fdfdd44-Paper-Conference.pdf#page=7)

作者尝试了投票和评分两种选择方法。评分方法使用结果奖励模型，英文缩写 ORM：它给完整解答打分，并用修正模型写出的答案来训练。对于前面 4×4 的安排，先从每条链的四份解答里选出一份，再在四条链选出的结果之间做选择。这里检查的是完整答案，与前一节 PRM 检查中间步骤、指导搜索的用途不同。[正式版附录 M–N](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/file/1b623663fd9b874366f3ce019fdfdd44-Paper-Conference.pdf#page=25)

sections.heading: 怎样知道一道题适合重新做，还是接着改
paragraphs: 作者先估计“这道题对当前模型有多难”。让模型对每题独立作答 2048 次，检查答对的比例，就能估计一次作答成功的概率，称为 pass@1。再按这个比例把题目分成五档。这样得到的难度与模型有关：同一道题，一个模型经常答对，另一个模型可能几乎做不出。这种分法使用了已知正确答案，所以论文称其为 oracle 难度，意思是借助了实际使用时未必拿得到的信息。[正式版 §3](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/file/1b623663fd9b874366f3ce019fdfdd44-Paper-Conference.pdf#page=4)

作者也做了不依赖标准答案的版本：仍生成这 2048 份解答，但用验证器的平均评分估计难度。知道难度后，再根据当前允许的计算量选择做法。在带验证器的修正实验里，较容易的题更适合连续修正；较难的题往往需要同时保留几种独立尝试，再分别修改。论文把这种“给定一道题和预算，选择较有效的用法”称为 compute-optimal。它是实验得到的近似策略，没有证明对所有题都最优，也没有解决多个用户之间应该怎样分配整台机器的计算量。

**一个重要限制是，这 2048 次试答和难度评分没有计入主要收益。** 即使不看标准答案，判断难度本身依然很贵。真实服务收到新问题后，还需要一种便宜的办法来决定采用哪种解法；否则为了节省后面的尝试，前面反而已经花了更多计算。论文展示了按难度选择的价值，但没有完成这一步部署问题。[正式版 Fig. 7、附录 E](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/file/1b623663fd9b874366f3ce019fdfdd44-Paper-Conference.pdf#page=18)

sections.heading: 实验里的 4× 收益，具体比较了什么
paragraphs: 先看实验对象。PaLM 2-S* 是作者使用的语言模型，也称为 Codey；MATH 是包含高中竞赛数学题的数据集。实验使用其中 12,000 道训练题和 500 道测试题。做搜索时，输入里还放了四份示例解答；用于检查和修正的模型也经过专门训练。因此这些结果对应的是这一整套设置，不能直接理解为任意模型多调用几次都会得到同样收益。[正式版 §4–6、附录 J](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/file/1b623663fd9b874366f3ce019fdfdd44-Paper-Conference.pdf#page=5)
修正实验中的 4× 表示：在图中某些比较点，按难度选择修正方式，用约四分之一的计算，就能超过独立作答后再选择的 best-of-N。这里省的是论文估算的计算量，不是说答对率变成四倍，也不是说实际 GPU 用时缩短到四分之一。搜索实验的 Fig. 4 则更谨慎：约四分之一预算能接近比较方法的效果。前一节提到的难度估计费用，仍然没有包含在里面。

读图还要留意一个版本细节：正式版把验证器的开销近似计为总计算翻倍。Fig. 6 图注写 128 对 512，§6.2 正文却写 64 对 256。两组数相差二倍，**与“只数解题生成”和“再算上检查费用”的区别一致，但这是我们的解释，原文没有把用词完全统一。** 因此不能把图上的 generation budget 一律读成实际生成了多少份答案，也不应在引用时把两个数字直接混用。[正式版 Fig. 4、6、§6.2](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/file/1b623663fd9b874366f3ce019fdfdd44-Paper-Conference.pdf#page=8)

sections.heading: 小模型多做几遍，什么时候能胜过大模型
paragraphs: 第 7 节把问题再往前推了一步：如果愿意花更多计算，是训练一个参数更多的模型，让它直接回答，还是保留小模型，让它每题多做几遍？参数就是训练得到的模型权重。训练费用在上线之前支付，大模型上线后的每次回答也更贵；小模型反复尝试的费用则随使用次数增加。因此必须同时计算训练和预期使用的总量，不能只比较某一道题的推理开销。

论文用 FLOPs 衡量计算量，也就是需要进行多少次浮点数运算；它不是秒数。还需要估计上线后要生成多少 token，即模型处理文字的基本单位。作者用 R 表示“上线后的生成 token 总量”除以“预训练读过的 token 总量”，实际比较 R=0.08、0.40、11。平均每次回答长度相同时，用户问得越多，R 就越大，训练成本也能由更多次使用共同承担。论文发现，较容易题或较少的预期使用量更有利于小模型多算；困难题或较大的使用量，则常更有利于大模型。[正式版 §7](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/file/1b623663fd9b874366f3ce019fdfdd44-Paper-Conference.pdf#page=10)
参数多约 14 倍的模型在这里采用 greedy 回答：生成每个 token 时都选当前概率最高的那个，直接得到一份答案。Fig. 8 的小模型策略又使用了前面借助标准答案得到的 oracle 难度。这个比较说明，在这些条件下，小模型增加计算有时更划算；它没有证明所有小模型都能战胜参数多 14 倍的模型。

**下面的公式用于核对预算，可以先跳过。** 比较时固定预训练 token 数，只改变参数量。设小模型参数量为 P，预训练 token 数为 Dpre，上线生成 token 数为 Dinf。会议版近似把训练计算记为 X=6P·Dpre，把推理计算记为 Y=4P·Dinf；后者已经包含验证器开销。若参数放大 M 倍，总计算按 M(X+Y) 估算。保持小模型训练不变、把余下预算留给它推理，则推理可放大到原来的 F=M+1.5(M−1)/R 倍。**纯粹代入举例**，M=14、R=1 时 F=33.5；这不是论文新增的实测点。公式要表达的是：同样的总预算能让小模型多做多少，取决于它以后要被使用多少次。

sections.heading: 回到服务系统：算得更少，为什么仍可能等得更久
paragraphs: **以下是根据执行过程做的系统分析，不是论文实测的 GPU 性能。** 回到那 16 份几何解答：如果独立开始 16 次，硬件允许时可以放在同一个批次里处理；如果先答一次、再连续修改 15 次，后一次必须等待前一次写完。于是，即使最后生成的文字一样多，用户等到最终答案的时间也可能不同。减少总运算次数，并不保证缩短这一串必须先后完成的工作。
显存需求也不一样。模型生成文字时，会缓存前面内容用于注意力计算的一部分中间结果，称为 KV cache，以减少后续重复计算。16 个独立尝试可能要同时保留更多份状态；连续修改则要处理输入里带着的旧答案。若几次尝试共享相同开头，部分缓存可能复用，但具体能省多少，要看引擎是否支持，以及各次输入究竟有多少相同内容。
检查答案同样需要运行模型，还可能排队或等待一批解答收齐。所以评估服务时，应在答对率相近的条件下，同时记录解题和检查的文字量、GPU 用时、峰值显存，以及半数请求和 95% 请求各能在多久完成，也就是 p50/p95 延迟。若换成会调用工具的 agent，还要算等待工具、暂停后恢复执行的时间；这些都不在本篇数学实验的测量范围里。

sections.heading: 怎样继续读，以及这篇还没有证明什么
paragraphs: 精读时可以按三个问题走。先读 §2–3 和 Fig. 5，搞清一次尝试会收到哪些输入、产生什么输出；再看 Fig. 3、6、7，比较容易题与困难题分别适合哪种做法；最后读 §7 和附录 E/G/M，检查解题之外的评分与难度判断有没有算进总计算量。每看到一条提升曲线，都问：这是多试了几种解法，还是把同一份答案改了更多次？最后是谁决定采用哪份答案？

本文的证据主要来自能检查最终答案的数学题。把方法搬到开放式研究任务时，怎样可靠地判断“这次更好了”本身就是问题。作者提出的后续方向是：把多次推理后得到的好答案拿去训练模型，使模型以后一次作答也能做得更好，再重复这个过程。这才涉及持续改变模型能力；它不同于这次回答时多试几遍。这样的循环是本文的未来设想，并不是已经验证成功的持续递归自我改进（recursive self-improvement，简称 RSI）。[正式版附录 A](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/file/1b623663fd9b874366f3ce019fdfdd44-Paper-Conference.pdf#page=16)

en.contribution: Separates test-time computation into changing the proposal distribution and searching with a verifier, then shows that choosing a strategy according to model-relative problem difficulty can use a budget more effectively than uniform best-of-N.
en.relevance: Provides a foundation for reasoning and test-time compute, while helping systems work distinguish search width, sequential dependencies, verifier overhead, and cache requirements. The paper need not be reduced to a serving application.
en.reading: Main reading for this edition; worth studying closely. Start with the two axes and the 16-attempt example, examine the difficulty and budget curves in Figures 3, 6, and 7, then audit the FLOPs assumptions in Section 7. Allow 40–60 minutes.
en.prerequisites: Autoregressive generation, sampling, and supervised finetuning. Pass@1 is single-attempt accuracy; a PRM scores intermediate steps, while an ORM scores a complete answer.
en.caveat: Uses the ICLR 2025 version: verifier overhead is included, but the 2,048-sample difficulty estimation is excluded. The 4× result is not measured GPU speedup, and the comparison against a 14× larger model depends on deployment volume and difficulty.

sections.heading: Start with a concrete question: where should extra computation go?
paragraphs: Snell, Lee, Xu, and Kumar ask how a fixed model should use additional inference budget on a particular problem: try again independently, revise an existing answer, or search through intermediate steps? The contribution is an analysis of when these choices help, rather than a new search algorithm that dominates on every problem. [Official ICLR 2025 record](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/hash/1b623663fd9b874366f3ce019fdfdd44-Abstract-Conference.html)

The 2024 preprint title ends with Scaling Model Parameters; the conference title ends with Scaling Parameters for Reasoning. This note follows the conference figures and compute accounting. Keep one distinction in mind throughout: making generation encounter a correct answer more often and reliably selecting that answer from the candidates are separate problems. [Preprint](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.03314); [conference Section 2](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/file/1b623663fd9b874366f3ce019fdfdd44-Paper-Conference.pdf#page=3)

sections.heading: Two axes: change where candidates come from, or how they are selected
paragraphs: The proposal distribution assigns probabilities to possible answers under the model's current conditioning. Independent resampling mostly buys additional attempts. Conditioning on previous answers and asking for revisions changes the distribution used for the next attempt. In these experiments, test-time changes concern inputs and candidate distributions: revision capability was finetuned beforehand, and weights are not updated separately for each test question. [Conference Sections 2–3](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/file/1b623663fd9b874366f3ce019fdfdd44-Paper-Conference.pdf#page=3)

The second axis is the verifier. It can rank completed solutions after generation, or score partial solutions to guide pruning and expansion. The former spends computation on covering possible approaches; the latter tries to stop unpromising branches earlier. These axes can be combined, but the paper's revision-plus-answer-selection experiments should not be mistaken for a joint optimization of revisions and PRM tree search.

sections.heading: Illustrative example: 16 attempts create three different execution shapes
paragraphs: **This is a teaching example, not a measured result from the paper.** Suppose the budget permits 16 complete attempts. A 16×1 allocation uses 16 independent starts; 1×16 uses one chain containing an initial answer and subsequent revisions; 4×4 uses four starts with four consecutive attempts in each chain. For now, count generations only. Answer lengths, historical context, and verifier costs will need separate accounting.

Imagine a geometry problem that admits either an auxiliary-line construction or a coordinate solution. A fully sequential chain might remain stuck with an unsuitable approach, while independent starts can cover alternatives. If the approach is sound and only one algebraic operation is wrong, revising may be more useful than starting over. This is an intuition for the results, not a guarantee that revisions are purely local. Answers must still be selected from the chain: its last output is not automatically its best. [Conference Figures 5 and 7](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/file/1b623663fd9b874366f3ce019fdfdd44-Paper-Conference.pdf#page=7)

sections.heading: The PRM predicts continuation success; it is not a proof checker
paragraphs: The authors continue sampling from intermediate solution steps, estimate a prefix's value from the fraction of continuations that finish correctly, and train the PRM on these soft labels. Appendix F uses 16 solutions per training question and 16 Monte Carlo continuations per step. A score therefore estimates the chance of eventual success under the base model's continuation policy. It is not a certificate that the current mathematical step is logically valid. [Conference Section 5.1 and Appendix F](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/file/1b623663fd9b874366f3ce019fdfdd44-Paper-Conference.pdf#page=19)

A completed solution is scored using the PRM's final-step prediction. Scores are then summed across solutions sharing the same final answer, and the answer with the greatest sum wins: best-of-N weighted. This differs from choosing the single highest-scoring solution and from equally weighted majority voting. **As an illustrative aggregation example**, two solutions ending in 12 with scores of 0.6 each outweigh one ending in 10 with a score of 0.9. [Appendix G](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/file/1b623663fd9b874366f3ce019fdfdd44-Paper-Conference.pdf#page=20)

sections.heading: Why more aggressive stepwise search can become worse
paragraphs: At each round, beam search scores partial solutions, retains promising prefixes, and branches from them to replenish the candidate pool. Lookahead adds a simulation: continue up to k steps and use the PRM score at that future prefix to evaluate the present choice. Better-informed selection is possible, but those trial continuations cost computation. The paper approximates this generation cost as N(k+1), rather than continuing to charge only N. [Conference Figure 2, Sections 5.2–5.3, and Appendix C](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/file/1b623663fd9b874366f3ce019fdfdd44-Paper-Conference.pdf#page=5)

In Figure 3, beam search helps at smaller budgets, but its advantage shrinks and sometimes reverses as the budget grows. The authors observe repetitive low-information steps and excessively short solutions, suggesting that search can exploit imperfections in the learned score. Optimizing a score harder does not necessarily improve actual correctness. Likewise, the reported lookahead results do not establish that every form of tree search is ineffective.

sections.heading: Where revision ability comes from, and why selection remains necessary
paragraphs: Revision training is more than adding a request to think again. The authors sample 64 responses per question in parallel, place up to four incorrect responses in context, and supervise a correct response as the target. An edit-distance heuristic helps choose a related incorrect answer, encouraging the model to use previous attempts. At inference, retaining only the latest four attempts allows the model to run longer revision chains. [Conference Section 6.1 and Appendix L](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/file/1b623663fd9b874366f3ce019fdfdd44-Paper-Conference.pdf#page=24)

Training contexts primarily contain mistakes, whereas an inference-time answer may already be correct. Continuing to revise introduces a distribution shift. In this setup, roughly 38% of correct answers are changed into incorrect ones, motivating majority or verifier-based selection. The revision experiments use an ORM adapted to revision-model outputs, selecting within each chain and then aggregating across chains. This is distinct from the earlier PRM-guided search. [Conference Section 6.1 and Appendices M–N](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/file/1b623663fd9b874366f3ce019fdfdd44-Paper-Conference.pdf#page=7)

sections.heading: Compute-optimal means conditioning the choice; estimating that condition is hard
paragraphs: Difficulty is relative to the model, rather than an intrinsic problem label. The oracle version estimates pass@1 from 2,048 samples per question and forms five difficulty bins. The predicted version instead averages verifier scores over those candidates, avoiding ground-truth answer labels. Difficulty and the available budget then determine the search method or sequential/parallel ratio. This is an empirical approximation to an ideal strategy, not a global optimality theorem or an implemented scheduler allocating resources across a multi-user queue. [Conference Section 3](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/file/1b623663fd9b874366f3ce019fdfdd44-Paper-Conference.pdf#page=4)

With verifier-based revision selection, easier questions favor more sequential computation, while harder ones benefit from balancing independent starts and subsequent revisions. **The major omission is that generating and scoring the 2,048 difficulty-estimation samples is excluded from the main compute comparison.** Predicted difficulty removes the dependency on true labels, but does not supply a cheap online router. A deployment must check whether estimating difficulty costs more than the inference computation it saves. [Conference Figure 7 and Appendix E](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/file/1b623663fd9b874366f3ce019fdfdd44-Paper-Conference.pdf#page=18)

sections.heading: The experiments and 4×: separate answer counts from adjusted budgets
paragraphs: The main experiments use PaLM 2-S* (Codey) and a MATH split with 12,000 training and 500 test questions. Search uses a four-example prompt; the PRM and revision model are separately finetuned. This is not a demonstration that an arbitrary base model improves simply by being put in a loop. The conference version explicitly approximates verifier overhead as doubling computation, so plotted generation budgets should not automatically be read as counts of completed candidate answers. [Conference Sections 4–6 and Appendix J](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/file/1b623663fd9b874366f3ce019fdfdd44-Paper-Conference.pdf#page=5)

For revisions, 4× describes exceeding parallel best-of-N near selected budgets using less computation. Figure 6's caption gives 128 versus 512; Section 6.2 gives 64 versus 256. Their factor-of-two difference is consistent with charging for the verifier. This is an interpretation of two counting conventions; the prose does not harmonize its terminology. For search, Figure 4 describes approximately matching the baseline with roughly one-quarter of the budget. Neither result means four times the accuracy or four times measured speed, and neither includes the difficulty-estimation cost above. [Conference Figures 4 and 6, Section 6.2](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/file/1b623663fd9b874366f3ce019fdfdd44-Paper-Conference.pdf#page=8)

sections.heading: The 14× larger model comparison: deployment volume changes the arithmetic
paragraphs: Section 7 matches total pretraining plus expected inference FLOPs, holding pretraining tokens fixed while increasing parameters. Let P denote parameters, Dpre training tokens, and Dinf inference tokens. The conference convention is X=6P·Dpre and Y=4P·Dinf, with the latter including approximate verifier overhead. Increasing parameters by M yields a budget of M(X+Y). Keeping the smaller model's training unchanged allows its inference budget to grow by F=M+1.5(M−1)/R, where R=Dinf/Dpre. [Conference Section 7](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/file/1b623663fd9b874366f3ce019fdfdd44-Paper-Conference.pdf#page=10)

**For an algebraic illustration**, M=14 and R=1 give F=33.5; this is not an additional measured point. At fixed average response length, more deployment queries increase Dinf and R, amortizing a one-time pretraining investment over more use. The paper evaluates R=0.08, 0.40, and 11. Easier questions or lower deployment volume more often favor additional small-model inference; hard questions and greater volume often favor the larger model. Figure 8 uses oracle difficulty and a greedy large-model baseline. It does not establish that any small model can beat one with 14 times as many parameters.

sections.heading: The systems interpretation: minimizing FLOPs does not guarantee the fastest response
paragraphs: **The following is systems reasoning, not a GPU measurement from the paper.** Return to the 16-attempt example: independent branches may be batched together, whereas each revision must wait for its predecessor. Equal generated-token totals can therefore have different critical paths. Parallel branches also require more active KV state, while sequential revisions must handle carried-forward historical context. Actual prefix sharing and context changes determine how much caching can save.

Verifier placement, batching, queueing, and synchronization for intermediate scores also affect latency and utilization. A serving evaluation should jointly measure accuracy, generation and verification tokens, GPU time, end-to-end p50/p95 latency, and peak memory, then compare cost at matched quality. Extending the workload to tool-using agents additionally requires external waiting and recoverable execution state. These stages were not measured in the mathematical reasoning experiments.

sections.heading: A reading route that turns the claims into checks
paragraphs: Begin with Sections 2–3 and Figure 5, drawing how candidates are generated and selected. Next read Figures 3, 6, and 7 to see whether different difficulty groups support one universal strategy. Finish with Section 7 and Appendices E/G/M to audit missing costs and aggregation rules. For every curve, ask what supplies the score, whether extra computation buys independent exploration or sequential depth, and whether its horizontal axis includes verification and routing costs.

This is a useful foundation for reasoning research, but its evidence centers on verifiable mathematics and does not automatically extend to open-ended research tasks. Distilling better inference outputs back into the model and repeating the cycle is a future direction in Appendix A, rather than a demonstrated sustained recursive self-improvement process. When reading later RSI work, look separately for evidence of better inference, weight updates, and net gains across multiple rounds. [Conference Appendix A](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/file/1b623663fd9b874366f3ce019fdfdd44-Paper-Conference.pdf#page=16)

papers.title: Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models

zh.contribution: 让同一个模型多做几次同一道题，再选择出现次数最多的答案。它不用额外训练一个打分模型，但需要支付多次作答的计算成本。
zh.relevance: 适合先理解“多算一会儿”究竟在做什么：一题同时生成多份解答，会增加输出文字、GPU 内存占用和等待时间，也可能提高答对的机会。
zh.reading: 建议用 25–35 分钟阅读。先用铅笔例子理解计票，再看 §2、图 1 和图 2；最后核对 §3.1–3.2 的实验条件与 §3.5 的结果。
zh.prerequisites: 正文会解释模型如何逐小段生成文字、为什么同一道题能产生不同回答，以及“先写解题过程再给答案”的提示方法，无须先熟悉相关缩写。
zh.caveat: 很多回答同意一个答案，不保证这个答案正确。论文主要结果每题生成 40 份解答；准确率提高时也花了更多计算，不能直接套用为当前模型在相同成本下的提升。

sections.heading: 先看它做了什么：同一道题多答几次，再数票
paragraphs: 假设我们问模型：“三盒铅笔，每盒四支，另有两支，共多少支？”只问一次，模型可能答对，也可能算错。这篇论文的办法是让同一个模型独立回答多次，最后数一数哪个答案出现得最多。这里的“独立”是说后一次不把前一次回答作为参考；它们仍出自同一个模型，可能犯相似的错误。

Self-Consistency 发表于 [ICLR 2023](https://iclr.cc/virtual/2023/poster/11718)，预印本发表于 2022 年。它改变的是一次请求要生成多少份回答、怎样选出最后的答案，不重新训练模型。模型权重是训练得到、决定模型如何计算的一组数值；这些数值在本方法的作答过程中保持不变。它也不额外训练一个 verifier，也就是专门判断解答好坏的模型。

sections.heading: 同一个模型怎样给出不同解答，又怎样选出一个答案
paragraphs: 先在输入中放入几道示范题，每道都写出解题过程和最终答案，让模型照这个格式回答新题。这种“先给少量例子”的做法叫 few-shot 提示；示例中包含解题过程，则称为思维链提示，英文缩写 CoT。这里说的思维链是模型写出来的文字，不代表我们已经知道它内部实际怎样完成计算。
模型生成文字时，每次输出一个 token，可以把它理解为一个字、一个词或词的一部分。模型会为可能接着出现的 token 给出概率。若每次都选概率最大的那个，就是 greedy decoding，中文常称贪心解码；若按这些概率随机选取，就叫采样。同一个输入经过多次采样，因而可能得到不同的解题过程与答案。
设生成了 K 份解答，K 就是尝试次数。程序从每份解答里取出最终答案，给相同答案各记一票，再选票数最高者。虽然常叫“多数投票”，最高票不必超过总票数的一半。三份解答即使分别用乘法、连加或先合并两盒，只要最后都是 14，就给 14 计三票。[原文 §2](https://arxiv.org/html/2203.11171#S2)
基础方法只数答案，不比较哪篇长解释的生成概率最高，也不让几个模型互相辩论。论文另比较了让每票带不同权重的方案。真正实现时还要处理一些细节：把“14”和“14 支”看成同一个答案吗？一份回答没有明确的最后答案怎么办？这些约定会直接影响票数。

sections.heading: 五份回答里三份选 14，能说它有六成把握吗
paragraphs: **沿用教学例子，以下不是论文实验：**五次回答依次是 14、10、14、12、14。程序会选 14，因为它有三票。正确答案也确实是 3×4+2=14，但这个例子只能说明计票过程，不能证明这种选择永远可靠。
三票除以五票得到 60%，意思只是“这五份回答中有六成给出了 14”。它不自动等于“14 有六成概率正确”。同一个模型可能一直漏掉题目里“另有两支”，于是五份回答全是 12；即便五票一致，答案仍然错误。
要把某个分数称为可信的把握程度，需要另外检查：在大量被报为“六成把握”的题目中，最后是否确实约有六成答对。这类对应关系叫校准。论文观察到答案越一致，通常越容易答对，但没有因此保证票数比例已经校准。若想根据票数提前停止生成，或决定“这题我不回答”，还需要在实际要处理的题目上单独测试。

sections.heading: 从一份回答变成 K 份，服务系统要多做哪些事
paragraphs: **以下是系统分析，不是论文测得的加速结果。** K 份回答可以同时计算，系统也可能把它们放进同一批 GPU 运算。它们读取的题目和示例相同，支持共享前缀的引擎可能复用这部分 KV cache：这是模型为已读文字保存的中间计算结果，用来避免生成下一个 token 时重复计算。开始写出不同内容后，每份回答仍需要保存自己的后续状态并继续计算。
同时运行 K 份回答不一定要等 K 倍时间，但也不会免费。它们会多生成文字、占用更多显存；有些解答写得更长，如果必须等全部回答齐了才能投票，最慢的那一份就会影响返回时间。因此比较方法时，要一起记录答对率、总输出 token 数、显存最高占用，以及用户从发问到拿到答案等了多久。
可以做一个很小的对照实验：固定同一批题、同一个模型、同一段提示和同一种答案提取程序，只改变 K。既记录单份回答的正确率，也记录投票后的正确率，并单独统计没有提取出答案、平票和超时的情况。准确率要用另外保留的评估题与标准答案计算；实际服务未知问题时，系统没有标准答案可直接核对。
如果加上“票数足够集中就提前结束”，应把它作为另一种方法单独比较。提前结束不仅减少了计算，也使尚未完成的回答失去投票机会，可能改变最终选出的答案。

sections.heading: 论文提高了多少准确率，又多做了多少次作答
paragraphs: 论文在 UL2、LaMDA、PaLM 和 GPT-3 系列上进行实验，都先提供少量解题示例，不额外训练模型。主要结果每次对每道题生成 40 份解答，再把评测独立重复 10 次取平均；对照方法是同样给出 CoT 示例，但用贪心解码只生成一份解答。这里的 10 次重复用于观察结果是否稳定，不是把 400 份回答合在一起投一次票。

在 GSM8K 数学题上，PaLM-540B 从 56.5% 提高到 74.4%，提高了 17.9 个百分点。这一设置使用八个算术示例，温度为 0.7，top-k 为 40。温度是调节采样随机程度的参数；top-k=40 表示每次生成下一个 token 时，只从概率最高的 40 个选项里采样。[原文 §3.1–3.2、表 2](https://arxiv.org/html/2203.11171#S3)
这些成绩是在增加作答次数之后得到的，不是两种方法消耗相同数量 token 的比较，也不表示每道题都得到改善。方法还需要能判断哪些最终答案算相同：自由写作、代码或有多种合理答案的任务，不能简单地把文字相同的回答算一组。模型若几乎从来写不出正确解法，多问几次也可能只是多收集一些相似错误。

sections.heading: 阅读时，先把“怎样选”与“花了多少”分开
paragraphs: 先读 §2 和图 1，用铅笔例子手工完成一次计票；再读图 2，看尝试次数增加时，准确率还能提高多少。接着核对 §3.1–3.2 的模型、提示和采样设置，最后读 §3.5，看看答案一致程度与正确率之间到底有什么联系。
读完可以用两个问题检查自己：把 K 翻倍后，多生成了多少文字，又要多等多久？如果某个答案获得绝大多数票，有没有独立的评估结果证明它更可靠？前一个问题帮助算成本，后一个问题帮助判断这些成本是否值得。

en.contribution: Samples multiple reasoning paths from one model and aggregates their final answers by vote count, trading extra inference computation for accuracy on reasoning tasks without training an additional verifier.
en.relevance: A clear starting point for parallel inference-time computation: multiple branches per question change total generated tokens, KV occupancy, batching, and completion latency.
en.reading: Worth a close read of the method and budget curves, about 25–35 minutes. Start with §2 and Fig. 1, then the setup in §3.1–3.2 and Fig. 2, and finish with the consistency analysis in §3.5.
en.prerequisites: Greedy decoding, temperature sampling, and CoT prompting; distinguish token probabilities, answer vote counts, and measured accuracy.
en.caveat: The most frequent answer can be wrong, and vote share is not calibrated model confidence. The original results use specific models, prompts, and 40 samples; they do not establish equal-cost gains for current models.

sections.heading: Two-minute overview: turn one answer into multiple attempts
paragraphs: Self-Consistency is an [ICLR 2023 paper](https://iclr.cc/virtual/2023/poster/11718), first released as a 2022 preprint. It gives a fixed model several attempts and aggregates their answers. It neither updates the weights nor trains an additional verifier, a model that judges candidates. This makes it a useful first reading on inference-time computation: locate the extra work before asking whether the gain justifies it.

sections.heading: Mechanism: sample reasoning paths and count final answers
paragraphs: Using the same prompt containing worked reasoning examples, sample K outputs, each containing a reasoning path and a final answer. Extract the answers, count their occurrences, and choose the most frequent. Although commonly called majority voting, the winner need not receive more than half the votes. Different calculations can count toward the same normalized answer. [Paper §2](https://arxiv.org/html/2203.11171#S2)

The aggregation operates on answers. It does not simply select the long output with the highest token likelihood, nor does it arrange a debate between models. Probability weighting is another option discussed in the paper; the basic version counts votes. An implementation needs explicit rules for answer formats, equivalent answers, and extraction failures because these affect the counts.

sections.heading: Teaching example: three correct votes do not imply 60% confidence
paragraphs: **Teaching example, not a paper experiment:** A question asks for the number of pencils in three boxes of four, plus two loose pencils. Five samples answer 14, 10, 14, 12, and 14, so aggregation selects 14. The three successful paths might use multiplication, repeated addition, or combine two boxes first; the implementation only needs to extract the same final quantity.

The fraction 3/5 describes these samples, not a calibrated 60% probability of correctness. One model can repeatedly make the same mistake, including a unanimous wrong answer. The paper observes an empirical relationship between consistency and accuracy. Using that relationship to abstain or stop sampling still requires evaluation on the target task; a vote count is not automatically calibrated confidence.

sections.heading: Systems connection: what multiple branches cost
paragraphs: **Systems analysis:** Expanding a prompt into K generation requests creates batching opportunities. An engine with prefix sharing may reuse KV for the identical prefix. Once branches generate different tokens, their subsequent KV and decode work remain necessary. This is an implementation implication, not a cache-speedup result measured by this paper.

Compare accuracy alongside total output tokens, peak memory, and request completion latency. K parallel requests neither cost nothing nor necessarily take K times the wall-clock time. Unequal branch lengths create tail waiting that can determine when a vote becomes available. Under a finite budget, compare several K values rather than presenting only the highest accuracy.

A minimal reproduction can fix the evaluation questions, prompts, model, and answer parser while varying the sample count. Record both single-response and aggregated accuracy, with extraction failures, ties, and timeouts reported separately. Early stopping is a different strategy that needs its own comparison: it changes which candidates can participate as well as reducing work. Gold test answers are unavailable during online inference; use a held-out offline evaluation set to measure accuracy.

sections.heading: Evidence and limits: keep the sampling budget attached to the gain
paragraphs: The paper runs few-shot experiments with UL2, LaMDA, PaLM, and GPT-3 variants. Main results average ten independent runs of 40 samples against greedy CoT. On GSM8K, PaLM-540B rises from 56.5% to 74.4%, a 17.9-percentage-point gain, with temperature 0.7, top-k 40, and eight arithmetic exemplars. [Paper §3.1–3.2, Table 2](https://arxiv.org/html/2203.11171#S3)

This does not show a benefit for every question or compare equal token budgets. Final answers must be meaningfully grouped: free-form writing, code, or tasks with several valid solutions cannot simply use raw-string voting. If correct answers are rarely produced, more samples may still fail; repeatedly sampling similar errors does not create independent evidence.

sections.heading: Reading path: count one vote before inspecting the budget curve
paragraphs: Start with three concepts: greedy decoding selects the highest-probability token at each step; temperature sampling permits varied outputs; CoT prompts demonstrate reasoning followed by an answer. Then hand-count the votes using §2 and Fig. 1, inspect varying sample counts in Fig. 2, and finish with §3.5. Ask how many extra tokens doubling K consumes, and how to test whether concentrated votes are more reliable. These questions connect serving cost to answer quality.

zh.contribution: 让模型先生成多份数学解答，再训练另一个模型来挑选。论文比较“只用最终答对与否教它”和“逐步指出对错教它”两种训练方式，并公开了 PRM800K 步骤标记数据。
zh.relevance: 多生成几份解答后，还需要决定相信哪一份。这篇解释负责挑选的模型怎样训练，以及为什么最后答对的解答也可能包含错误过程。
zh.reading: 值得精读。先看下文的方程例子，再读 §2.1、§2.4–2.6；最后对照图 3–4 和附录 C/F，核对训练方式、测试题与尝试次数。
zh.prerequisites: 正文会解释怎样用人工对错标记训练一个打分模型，以及怎样先生成 N 份解答、再按分数选一份；不要求预先掌握奖励模型术语。
zh.caveat: 78.2% 是在专门保留的 500 道题上，每题生成 1860 份解答后再挑选的成绩。论文研究怎样挑得更准，没有进一步用这些分数做强化学习来训练作答模型。

sections.heading: 先有很多份解答，再训练一个负责挑选的模型
paragraphs: 一道题如果已经有多份解答，我们该相信哪一份？[这篇 ICLR 2024 论文](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/file/aca97732e30bcf1303bc22ac3924fd16-Paper-Conference.pdf)把工作分给两个角色：一个模型负责写解答，称为生成器；另一个模型负责看解答、打分，称为奖励模型。分数越高，表示后者越倾向于认为这份解答值得选。
论文比较的是怎样训练第二个模型。评估时，负责作答的生成器固定不变；研究者让它为每道题写 N 份解答，然后让奖励模型选分数最高的一份。这种“从 N 份里挑一份”的办法叫 best-of-N。§2.1 明确说明，论文没有继续用奖励分数做强化学习，也就是没有靠“答得好就获得更高奖励”的反馈去更新作答模型。
**阅读时可以这样检查问题：**如果 N 份解答里根本没有正确的，再好的挑选方法也选不出正解。如果里面已经有正确解答，却仍选中了错误的，就要检查打分模型。增加 N 之前，应分别数清“有多少题至少出现过一份正解”和“有多少题最后真的选中了正解”。

sections.heading: 只检查最后的答案，与逐步检查过程，有什么区别
paragraphs: **教学例子，不是论文样例：**解 2x+3=11。一份解答先得到 2x=8，再得到 x=4；另一份先错写成 2x=6，接着毫无根据地写出 x=4。如果只把最后的 x=4 与标准答案比较，两份都可能被记为“正确”。检查过程才会发现第二份在中间算错了。
把这样的解答记成“对”或“错”，叫标注；写下的对错记录叫标签。第一种训练方式只根据最终答案是否正确给整份解答贴标签，再教奖励模型预测这个标签，称为结果监督，模型简称 ORM。ORM 仍然能读完整篇解答，“结果监督”说的是老师给它什么标签，不是它只能看到最后一个数字。

第二种方式请人逐步检查，告诉模型哪个步骤合理、哪个步骤错误，称为过程监督，模型简称 PRM。本文使用正、负、中性三种步骤标签，主要的数据收集流程在遇到第一个错误步骤后停止标注。这样，训练模型时不只知道“这份解答有错”，还知道错误从哪里开始。[§2.4–2.6](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/file/aca97732e30bcf1303bc22ac3924fd16-Paper-Conference.pdf#page=3)
把解答和人工标签配成训练样例，让模型练习预测这些标签，就是这里的监督训练，也是一种监督微调，常写作 SFT。训练会调整模型权重，即决定模型计算方式的一组数值，让它更容易预测出训练样例给定的标签。但学过逐步对错，不等于它就能抓住所有错误；上面的方程例子只是说明两种训练方式给了不同信息。

sections.heading: 每一步都有分数以后，怎样给整份解答排序
paragraphs: 训练好的 PRM 会在每个步骤结束的位置，预测它属于正、负或中性标签的概率。让模型对整份解答做一次前向计算，也就是输入文字、算出预测结果，就能得到各步骤的分数；不必让它针对每一步再写一段长篇批评。

用于最终排序时，作者把中性也算作可接受，因此每步的分数是“正类概率加中性概率”。再把一份解答里各步的这个分数相乘，得到整份解答的分数。附录 F 还比较了另一种做法：不相乘，只取最差那一步的分数。[附录 F](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/file/aca97732e30bcf1303bc22ac3924fd16-Paper-Conference.pdf#page=15)
**继续用教学分数举例：**把一份解答写成三个步骤，A 的分数是 0.95、0.90、0.95，相乘约为 0.812；B 的分数是 0.99、0.30、0.99，相乘约为 0.294。即使 B 的开头和结尾得分很高，中间那个低分也会拉低总分。这个例子说明为什么逐步检查可能帮助排除“中途算错、最后碰巧答对”的解答。
这些分数依然只是模型的判断，不是数学证明。它报出 0.9，是否真的意味着类似步骤中约九成正确，需要用另外的数据检验；这种检查叫概率校准。此外，同一段解释被拆成更多步骤，会多乘几个不超过 1 的数，也可能降低总分。复现时必须记清怎样划分步骤、中性如何处理、最后怎样计算总分，不能只记“用了 PRM”。

sections.heading: 78.2% 是怎样测出来的
paragraphs: 大规模实验使用从 GPT-4 基础模型进一步训练得到的生成器和奖励模型，处理 MATH 数学题。公开的 PRM800K 数据包含约 80 万条人工步骤标签。作者从原 MATH 测试集中随机留出 500 道题进行评估，将其余 4500 道题用于收集训练相关数据。因此，这里的测试范围是这 500 道保留题，不能当成未经调整的完整 MATH 测试集。

图 3 的 **78.2%** 表示：每道保留题先生成 **1860 份解答**，由 PRM 打分并选出一份，再检查这份解答的最终答案。相同评测设置下，用 ORM 挑选得到 72.4%，按最终答案多数投票得到 69.6%。78.2% 不是只让模型答一次就能达到的正确率；阅读成绩时，要把 best-of-1860 的计算量一起记住。[§2–3、附录 C](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/file/aca97732e30bcf1303bc22ac3924fd16-Paper-Conference.pdf#page=5)
大规模 PRM 与 ORM 还使用了不同的训练数据，所以不能把全部分数差距都解释为“逐步标对错”这一项改动造成。论文另做了一组较小模型的实验：让较大的 PRM 提供训练标签，在相同训练解答上比较不同的监督方式。这更接近只改变一个条件的比较，但提供标签的大模型也可能犯错。两组实验回答的问题不同，都没有给出可直接套用到当前部署上的 GPU 延迟提升倍数。

sections.heading: 为什么专挑“看着像对、实际上答错”的解答请人检查
paragraphs: 假设 PRM 已经能轻易看出“2+2=7”有问题，再让人反复标记这类明显错误，未必能教会它多少新东西。作者更希望找到这样的解答：当前 PRM 给了高分，最终答案却是错的。请人检查这些解答，就有机会指出模型没看出来的具体错误，再把它们加入训练。

这种有选择地决定下一批检查什么数据的做法叫主动学习。§2.4 描述了实际收集数据时的选择方式；§4 又用较小模型做对照实验，并让大 PRM 提供标签。后者说明某种选题方式可能用较少训练样例得到相近成绩，但不能直接换算成“完整人工标注流程都便宜了同一个倍数”。[§2.4、§4](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/file/aca97732e30bcf1303bc22ac3924fd16-Paper-Conference.pdf#page=6)
**如果据此设计自己的实验：**应另留一批没有用于挑题或训练的评估题，记录新增数据分别补了哪些错误，也记录标签是谁给的。只在刚刚加入训练的难题上变好，可能只是更熟悉这些题；若一直由同一个模型提供训练标签、再由它判断效果，就容易把它自己的偏差当成进步。

sections.heading: 这篇能帮我们做什么，又没有证明什么
paragraphs: 今天的主读讨论“多出来的计算怎样分配”，这篇补充的是“如果要请一个模型检查答案，怎样把它训练出来”。多写几份解答有没有用，既取决于能否写出正解，也取决于能否把正解选出来。先区分这两件事，才知道该改进作答模型还是检查模型。
**系统分析：**多运行一个 PRM 需要额外计算和显存。如果把评分放进逐步搜索里，下一步扩展还可能必须等评分完成。因此，判断方法是否值得部署，应在相同答题质量下比较总 GPU 时间、费用，以及最慢一批请求要等多久；打分更准，不直接等于返回更快。
数学题通常有较容易核对的最终答案，但让 Agent 完成开放任务时，每一步是否合理往往更难判断。而且，模型写出来的步骤获得 PRM 认可，也不证明这些文字忠实描述了它内部的计算过程。
建议先读 §2.1，确认作答模型和打分模型的分工；再看图 3–4，分清两组训练比较；最后看附录 C/F，检查测试题怎么留、分数怎么算。读完问自己：多生成答案仍没有提高最终正确率，是从未生成正解，还是正解被打了低分，或者整份解答的分数算法有问题？这三个问题可以分别检查。

en.contribution: Compares outcome and process supervision for reward models, showing how step-level feedback helps select reliable solutions, and releases PRM800K.
en.relevance: Explains who selects among generated candidates, connecting inference-time search, reward modeling, and evaluation.
en.reading: Read §2.1, §2.4–2.6, Figures 3–4, and Appendices C/F closely. Establish the supervised object and evaluation budget before interpreting scores.
en.prerequisites: Classification, conditional probability, supervised fine-tuning, and best-of-N selection from N generated candidates.
en.caveat: Primarily evaluates mathematical answer selection with a fixed generator, not a policy trained by PRM-based RL; 78.2% uses a specific 500-problem split and best-of-1860.

sections.heading: The trained object is the judge, not an RL-updated generator
paragraphs: The [ICLR 2024 paper](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/file/aca97732e30bcf1303bc22ac3924fd16-Paper-Conference.pdf) studies reliable reward models. A generator produces candidate solutions, a reward model scores them, and one is selected. Section 2.1 explicitly excludes reinforcement learning of the generator. Process supervision here is therefore a training signal for the judge; it does not establish that an RL policy has learned to reason correctly at every step.

This separates two failures: selection cannot recover a correct solution that never appears, whereas choosing incorrectly when a correct candidate exists points toward evaluation and ranking. **Our reading inference:** before increasing N, inspect both candidate coverage and selected-answer accuracy. Candidate count alone cannot identify where additional compute would be useful.

sections.heading: ORM and PRM differ in the granularity of supervision
paragraphs: An outcome-supervised reward model (ORM) learns from final-result correctness. It can still read the entire solution; outcome supervision does not mean reading only the last number. A process-supervised reward model (PRM) learns step acceptability. Human feedback in this work uses positive, negative, and neutral labels, stopping at the first error. Step labels locate a failure; an outcome label usually says only that the whole attempt failed. [§2.4–2.6](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/file/aca97732e30bcf1303bc22ac3924fd16-Paper-Conference.pdf#page=3)

**Teaching example, not a paper example:** solving 2x + 3 = 11 correctly gives 2x = 8 and x = 4. Another trajectory mistakenly writes 2x = 6, then jumps without justification to x = 4. Checking only the final answer may label both correct; checking the derivation exposes the break. This illustrates feedback granularity, not a guarantee that a learned PRM catches every such error.

sections.heading: Turning step scores into a solution score
paragraphs: The model predicts labels at step boundaries. One forward pass over a complete solution can provide the boundary scores; this need not mean generating a separate lengthy critique of every step. For ranking, the authors treat neutral steps as acceptable and multiply step-acceptability probabilities. Appendix F compares alternatives including minimum aggregation. [Appendix F](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/file/aca97732e30bcf1303bc22ac3924fd16-Paper-Conference.pdf#page=15)

**Teaching example:** candidate A has scores 0.95, 0.90, and 0.95, whose product is approximately 0.812. Candidate B has 0.99, 0.30, and 0.99, yielding approximately 0.294. B's weak middle step sharply reduces its rank. These remain model scores, not formal correctness certificates. Multiplication is sensitive to calibration and step count: splitting the same explanation into more steps can change its score. Reproduction should record segmentation, label handling, and aggregation together.

sections.heading: Read the result together with the candidate budget
paragraphs: Large-scale experiments use generator and reward models derived from base GPT-4 on MATH, with roughly 800,000 step labels in PRM800K. The authors use 4,500 problems from the original MATH test split for training-related data and evaluate on the remaining 500 randomly held-out problems. Figure 3 reports **78.2% for PRM selection among 1,860 candidates per problem**, compared with 72.4% for ORM and 69.6% for majority voting. This is neither single-sample accuracy nor a result on the untouched full MATH test split. [§2–3 and Appendix C](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/file/aca97732e30bcf1303bc22ac3924fd16-Paper-Conference.pdf#page=5)

Large-scale PRM and ORM training data differ, so their entire performance gap cannot be attributed to switching label granularity alone. Separate smaller-model comparisons use synthetic supervision from a larger PRM while controlling training samples. Keep these evidence types separate: one compares strong implementations, while the other attempts to isolate supervision and depends on teacher-label quality. The paper supplies no end-to-end GPU latency multiplier that can simply be applied to a present-day deployment.

sections.heading: Why informative negatives can beat more obvious errors
paragraphs: Collection prioritizes candidates that the current PRM scores highly but whose final answers are wrong, so annotators can expose the judge's blind spots. This differs from repeatedly adding examples it already finds easy to reject. Section 4 studies active selection with smaller models; its sample-efficiency result should not be treated as a universal reduction in complete human-labeling cost. [§2.4 and §4](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/file/aca97732e30bcf1303bc22ac3924fd16-Paper-Conference.pdf#page=6)

**Our experimental-design suggestion, not a paper result:** an analogous feedback loop should independently hold out evaluation tasks and record which error types each iteration adds. Fixing selected training cases may reflect adaptation to that distribution. A verifier producing labels and then judging its own progress can also make improvements appear more robust than independent tests would support.

sections.heading: Connection to the main reading and limits of transfer
paragraphs: Today's main reading asks how to allocate inference compute; this paper explains where a trained verifier can come from. Generator quality, verifier quality, candidate count, and task success must be considered together. **Systems analysis:** a PRM adds model execution and memory demand, and stepwise search can introduce synchronization barriers. Compare total GPU time, tail latency, and cost at the same quality target rather than equating more accurate judging with faster serving.

Automatically checkable mathematics does not make every step of an open-ended agent task easy to label. Approval of a textual step also does not establish that the text faithfully describes the model's internal computation. Read §2.1 for the research object, Figures 3–4 for the experimental comparisons, and Appendices C/F for splits and scoring. Then ask: when more candidates stop improving selected-answer accuracy, should we inspect generation coverage, judge errors, or aggregation? These distinctions transfer better than memorizing 78.2%.

zh.contribution: 先让模型写解题过程，保留最终答对的解答，用它们继续训练；对原先答错的题，先提示标准答案，再尝试补出可用的训练解答。
zh.relevance: 能看清生成、检查和训练怎样连起来，也能帮助规划训练系统：生成得快还不够，要看最后留下多少可学习的解答，以及它们花了多少时间。
zh.reading: 建议约 30 分钟，作为“多次作答后选择答案”之外的另一条路线。先读 §3 和算法 1，再核对 §4.1、表 1，最后看 §5–6 对错误解释和方法局限的讨论。
zh.prerequisites: 需要区分“告诉模型怎样回答”和“用数据训练模型”。正文会解释模型权重与监督微调，也会说明每轮用谁生成数据、从谁开始训练。
zh.caveat: 标准答案提示只用于制作训练数据，正式训练输入与测试题都去掉这条提示。每轮从固定原始模型重新训练，而不是接着上一轮权重续训；最后答对也不能保证中间过程正确。

sections.heading: 先看目标：让这次写出的好解答帮助以后作答
paragraphs: 前一篇 Self-Consistency 让模型多答几次，目的是给当前这道题选一个答案。STaR 还想多走一步：把答对的解题过程保存下来，作为训练材料，让模型以后更容易写出类似的好解答。这篇论文发表于 [NeurIPS 2022](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2022/hash/639a9a172c044fbb64175b5fad42e9a5-Abstract-Conference.html)。
它需要大量已经知道标准答案的题目，只是这些题大多没有人工写好的解题过程。模型先尝试补出过程，研究者按最终答案筛选，再用留下来的解答训练模型。因此，“自己教自己”仍然用到了外部提供的正确答案。
这里的训练会改变模型权重，也就是训练得到、决定模型如何计算的一组数值。给定题目，让模型练习输出我们选好的“解题过程加答案”，逐渐提高它生成这些目标文字的概率，这种做法叫监督微调，英文缩写 SFT。它会改变模型以后的回答，与在一次请求中多问几遍是两回事。

sections.heading: 一轮具体怎么做：先自己答，失败后再提示答案
paragraphs: 首先，在输入里放入少量“题目、解题过程、答案”的示例，让当前模型按照这个格式回答训练题。这种先给少量示例的做法叫 few-shot 提示。把模型的最终答案与标准答案比较，答对的解答留下，准备作为训练数据。

对于没答对的题，再把标准答案告诉模型，请它重新尝试写出解题过程。论文把这种办法称为 rationalization：已知答案后尝试补出理由。即使已经提示了标准答案，第二次生成的最终答案仍要通过检查。普通作答留下的解答，加上这一路补救得到的合格解答，构成这一轮的训练材料。[正式论文 §3、算法 1](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2022/file/639a9a172c044fbb64175b5fad42e9a5-Paper-Conference.pdf#page=3)
还有一个容易看漏的细节：每轮都从同一个原始预训练模型 M 开始训练。第一轮由 M 写数据，再拿这些数据训练出 M₁；第二轮让 M₁ 写新数据，却重新取一份原始 M，用新数据训练出 M₂。于是，用来写数据的模型会逐轮变化，训练的起点始终是 M。方法把改进传进新数据，而不是直接接着上一轮权重一直训练。

sections.heading: 用铅笔题走一遍：标准答案何时出现，何时拿掉
paragraphs: **以下是教学例子，不是论文实验：**题目是“三盒铅笔，每盒四支，另有两支，共多少支？”第一遍模型答成 10，没有通过答案检查。制作训练数据时，我们告诉它正确答案是 14，它再写出：“三盒一共 3×4=12 支，再加两支，得到 14 支。”这份解答的最终答案通过检查，就可以留下。
真正拿这份解答训练模型时，要把输入里的“正确答案是 14”拿掉。训练输入不包含给这道题的答案提示；让模型学习输出的目标文字，则是上面那段过程和最终的 14。测试新题时，同样不给标准答案提示。这样训练的目的，是让模型以后从题目出发写出解答，而不是学会抄输入里已经给出的答案。
不过，第二次写出的理由也可能是编造的：模型可能乱算一通，最后照着提示写下 14，仍通过只检查最终答案的程序。因此，这个方法找到的是“最终答案正确的训练文字”，不能保证每一步都对。若需要可靠的过程，还要逐步检查；能用程序验证时就验证，不能时也应抽样请人检查。

sections.heading: 做成训练系统时，要分别记清数据和模型来自哪里
paragraphs: **以下是系统分析。**一轮有几件不同的工作：生成解答，核对最终答案，给失败题提示答案后再生成，合并通过检查的解答，最后训练。日志应记录每份解答来自哪个版本的模型、是哪道题、是否用过答案提示，以及最后有没有留下。这样下一轮效果变化时，才知道发生了什么。
还要分别保存“本轮负责写数据的模型”和“固定的训练起点 M”。只留一份名为“最新模型”的参数文件，会丢失这个区别，之后很难重现同一轮实验。
对强化学习基础设施的一个启发是：每秒写出多少份解答，不能代替每秒留下多少份可用于训练的解答。许多高速生成的回答可能都答错了；提示答案后再试，也要支付另一轮生成费用。可以分别记录普通作答留下多少题、补救多留下多少题，以及两部分各自消耗的 token 和时间。token 是模型处理文字的小单位，例如一个字、一个词或词的一部分。
即使两种方案最后留下同样多的数据，花费也可能很不一样。还要抽查留下来的解题过程，避免把“更容易猜中最后答案”误当成“更有学习价值”。这也连接到递归自我改进（RSI）的讨论：模型把自己产出的材料再用于训练。但本文依靠已知答案和固定任务，不能据此推出模型能一直改进，更不能推出它无需外部反馈。

sections.heading: 实验提高了多少，这些成绩说明到哪里
paragraphs: 作者使用 GPT-J 6B，也就是约 60 亿参数的模型，测试加法、CommonsenseQA 常识选择题和 GSM8K 数学题。CommonsenseQA 使用 9,741 道训练题，以及十个人工写有解题过程的示例。论文反复进行前面所说的数据生成与训练，直到成绩趋于稳定，并报告过程中最好的结果。

表 1 报告的是 CommonsenseQA **开发集**成绩。开发集是一批用来观察效果和选择设置的评估题，不应与最后独立报告的测试集混称。直接训练模型从题目输出答案，正确率为 **60.0%**；STaR 只保留自己答对的解答、不做答案提示补救，得到 **68.8%**；加入补救后，得到 **72.5%**。[正式论文 §4.1、表 1](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2022/file/639a9a172c044fbb64175b5fad42e9a5-Paper-Conference.pdf#page=5)
这些数字没有比较相同计算成本下哪种服务系统更快，也不是当前模型的排行榜。CommonsenseQA 是五选一题，模型即使解释错误，也可能碰巧选对，于是错误解释仍可能进入训练。原始模型还必须已经有一定的写解答能力，否则最初连足够的可用材料都得不到，后面的训练也难以开始。
因此，需要分别检查三件事：最后的答案是否更准，写出来的步骤是否更合理，换一类题目后是否还有效。一个开发集正确率，不能同时证明这三件事。

sections.heading: 读算法时，盯住两个模型角色和答案提示的位置
paragraphs: 先读 §3 和算法 1，用铅笔题走完“普通作答”和“提示答案后补救”两条路径。每次看到训练，都问它从哪份参数开始；每次看到生成，都问它用了哪一轮的模型。再核对 §4.1 与表 1 的实验条件，最后读 §5–6 对错误推理和方法边界的讨论。
读完应该能说明：标准答案提供了什么信息，哪些文字是模型自己生成的，答案提示在哪一步被拿掉。如果最后答案很容易猜中，筛选会留下什么错误材料？如果同一批题不断被用于训练，又应另外保留哪些题来检查真实进步？这些问题决定这种训练循环是否可信。

en.contribution: Uses a few reasoning examples to bootstrap generation, filters generated rationales against known answers, and uses answer hints to recover training examples from failures before iterative fine-tuning.
en.relevance: Connects inference generation to post-training through a rollout, filtering, and training loop, raising questions about data versions, usable-example yield, and resource allocation between stages.
en.reading: An optional contrast with pure inference-time computation, about 30 minutes. Read §3 and Algorithm 1 closely, then §4.1 and Table 1, and finish with the rationale-quality and bootstrapping limits in §5–6.
en.prerequisites: Supervised fine-tuning, answer-labeled datasets, and few-shot prompts; distinguish the model used to generate data from the checkpoint used to initialize training.
en.caveat: Rationalization uses gold answers while constructing training data, not during testing. Each round fine-tunes the fixed original model, and a correct final answer does not certify a correct reasoning process.

sections.heading: Two-minute overview: turn generated reasoning into training data
paragraphs: STaR is a [NeurIPS 2022 paper](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2022/hash/639a9a172c044fbb64175b5fad42e9a5-Abstract-Conference.html). Whereas Self-Consistency samples additional attempts within an inference request, STaR fine-tunes on generated reasoning and changes the model that answers future questions. It still requires many questions with correct final answers; most lack human-written rationales. Self-teaching here does not mean an absence of external supervision.

sections.heading: Mechanism: generate, filter, recover failures, then train from the fixed base
paragraphs: A few question–rationale–answer examples prompt the current model to generate rationales and answers for training questions. Correct answers are retained. Failed questions receive rationalization: the known answer becomes a hint for another attempt, whose final answer must still pass the check. Both sets form the next training dataset. [Conference paper §3, Algorithm 1](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2022/file/639a9a172c044fbb64175b5fad42e9a5-Paper-Conference.pdf#page=3)

Each round uses the preceding model to generate data but starts fine-tuning from the same original pretrained model M, rather than continually updating the previous round's weights. Improvement passes through the new data. The answer hint is removed from the training input of recovered examples: the model learns to produce reasoning and an answer from the question. Test questions also receive no gold-answer hint.

sections.heading: Teaching example: answer hints construct data, not test-time answers
paragraphs: **Teaching example, not a paper experiment:** The question again concerns three boxes of four pencils and two loose pencils. An initial attempt incorrectly answers 10. During data construction, the model is given the correct answer 14 and generates an explanation that first counts twelve boxed pencils and then adds two. If the final answer passes, the training input retains only the question, while the target is the rationale followed by 14.

This does not discover an unknown answer from nothing. It seeks a learnable process under existing answer supervision. A fabricated explanation could also end in 14, so answer matching filters outcomes only. Claims about trustworthy reasoning require additional step checks, executable verification where available, or human inspection; correct output and correct reasoning must remain separate criteria.

sections.heading: Systems connection: track data and model versions through the loop
paragraphs: **Systems analysis:** Decompose a round into generation, answer checking, recovery of failures, dataset assembly, and fine-tuning. Track the generating model version, question source, recovery flag, and filtering outcome to explain changes in the next round. A fixed training initialization and an evolving data-generation model represent different version relationships; storing only a latest checkpoint loses that distinction.

For RL infrastructure, generation throughput should be considered alongside usable-example yield. Fast incorrect generations need not produce more training data, and recovery consumes additional generation work. This also connects to recursive self-improvement, or RSI, but the feedback here comes from known answers and fixed tasks. It does not establish unlimited, unsupervised improvement.

Useful logs should count examples accepted from ordinary generation, additional examples recovered, and tokens and time spent on each path. Equal usable-example counts may have very different costs. Inspect the quality of retained rationales as well: optimizing acceptance rate alone can favor answers that are easy to guess instead of examples that are valuable to learn from.

sections.heading: Evidence and limits: development-set gains are not a universal reasoning guarantee
paragraphs: Experiments use GPT-J 6B on addition, CommonsenseQA, and GSM8K. CommonsenseQA supplies 9,741 training questions and ten manually written rationale examples. Table 1 reports development-set accuracy of 60.0% for direct-answer fine-tuning, 68.8% for STaR without rationalization, and 72.5% with it. The authors iterate until performance saturates and report the best results. [Conference paper §4.1, Table 1](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2022/file/639a9a172c044fbb64175b5fad42e9a5-Paper-Conference.pdf#page=5)

These are neither current-model rankings nor equal-compute serving comparisons. Five-way multiple-choice questions let guessed correct answers admit poor rationales into training. A base model unable to generate useful processes may also fail to bootstrap. Evaluate final-answer accuracy, rationale quality, and transfer separately; one development-set score cannot establish all three.

sections.heading: Reading path: draw two model roles and two data paths
paragraphs: First understand supervised fine-tuning as increasing the probability of a target text given its question. Then draw the ordinary-generation and answer-hint recovery paths from Algorithm 1, labeling the training arrow as initialized from M. Continue with §4.1, Table 1, and §5–6. Ask what information the gold answers provide, what process the model generates, how easy-to-guess answers undermine filtering, and how to preserve an independent evaluation set when training questions are reused.
